title: PROGNOSTIC VALUE OF ACTIN‐FREE GC‐GLOGULIN IN CHILDREN WITH ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
abstract: Actin released in the circulation upon cell death can induce intravascular coagulation and multi organ dysfunction. Gc-globulin, synthesised by the liver, is a key player in the extra-cellular actin scavenger system. Hence, low levels of actin-free Gc-globulin (AfGc) may serve as a prognostic marker of survival in acute liver failure (ALF). To evaluate the prognostic value of AfGc in paediatric ALF. Serum AfGc levels were measured using a rapid ELISA kit (Antibody Shop, Gentofte, Denmark) at admission in 115 children (60 male, median age 5.05 years, range 0-17.4) with ALF (INR >2 unresponsive to vitamin K and abnormal liver enzymes). Causes of ALF were: autoimmune hepatitis (10), drug-induced (16), haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (5), hypoxia (4), viral hepatitis (10), metabolic (14), neonatal haemochromatosis (7), veno-occlusive disease (2), Wilson disease (6), idiopathic (41). Fifty-eight patients survived with medical treatment only (Group-1); 20 died (Group-2); 37 were transplanted, of whom 26 survived (Group-3) and 11 died (Group-4). AfGc levels (μg/ml) were: Group 1: median 255 (range 0.2-525); Group 2: 105 (0.1-365); Group 3: 95 (0.1-355); Group 4: 85 (0.1-270), values being significantly higher in Group-1 when compared to Group-2 (p = 0.002) and to all the children who died or required transplantation taken together (p = 0.00001). At a cut off level of 190 μg/ml (obtained by plotting a receiver operative characteristic curve; the value of the area under the curve being 0.79), sensitivity and specificity for predicting survival with native liver were 85% and 62% respectively. These results show that AfGc levels on admission are of prognostic importance in children with ALF. Prospective studies with serial measurements are necessary to further elucidate the accuracy and practical value of this test.

title: CTLA‐4 GENE POLYMORPHISM AND THE OUTCOME OF AUTOIMMUNE HEPATITIS
abstract: A - G transition in ekson 1 (+49) of CTLA-4 gene may play a role in T-cells activation and may influence the treatment outcome in children with autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). THE AIM of the study was to evaluate the outcome of AIH therapy in children with different CTLA-4 genotypes. We analyzed 54 case records of children (M-13, F-41) with AIH diagnosed at the age of 2-16 (mean ± SD 10.7 ± 3.3) years and observed for 2-11 (5.4 ± 2.5) years after diagnosis. All children were treated with prednisone and azathioprine for the first two years after the diagnosis had been established. The subsequent therapy was modified according to the efficacy and tolerability. The treatment outcome assessment was based on the presence of clinical, laboratory, ultrasound and histopathological features of liver disease. The following categories of outcome were defined: full remission, partial remission or continuous disease. CTLA-4 polymorphism was analyzed by restriction analysis. CTLA-4 genotype AA was found in 19 (35%), AG in 26 (48%) and GG in 9 (17%) children. No differences in the liver function tests among different CTLA-4 genotypes were observed at presentation of the disease and at two years of treatment. At the end of observation period children with genotype AG presented with higher than children with genotypes AA or GG ALT activity (respectively 113 ± 156 U/l vs 64 ± 54 U/l and 51 ± 23 U/l, p = 0.04) and higher histopathological grading score (3.0 ± 0.8 vs 0.3 ± 0.6 and 0.7 ± 0.6, p = 0.02). Full AIH remission was observed in 12 (22%) and continuous disease was observed in 11 (20%) of children. Lack of therapeutic effect was observed more often in children with genotype AG than in those with genotypes AA or GG (respectively 30,8% vs 5,3% and 22,2%) but these differences were not statistically significant. 3 children required conversion to cyclosporine and 2 children had liver transplantation. All these children had genotype AG. Poor therapeutic effect was observed more often in children with CTLA-4 genotype AG.

title: EPIDEMIOLOGY OF INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE AMONG CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS IN CENTRAL AND WESTERN SLOVENIA: A 12‐YEAR RETROSPECTIVE STUDY (1994‐2005)
abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in children aged less than 18 years in central and western Slovenia and to compare the incidences of IBD during the 6-year-periods 1994-1999 and 2000-2005. We collected all the data for the 12-year-period 1994-2005 retrospectively from the patient charts in seven pediatric and gastroenterologic centers in central and western Slovenia. The demographic population figures are based on national registry data. IBD diagnosis was based on clinical assessment, endoscopy and histology. The childhood population of central and western Slovenia was 300.979 for the period 1994-1999 and 265.742 for the period 2000-2005; figures are based on the national population registry data. Incidence of all types of childhood IBD in central and western Slovenia is high and is still rising. Our data is comparable to incidence figures for other western and central European countries. The rise of incidence of UC and IC appears to be higher than the rise of incidence of CD. Nevertheless, CD still remains the most prevalent type of IBD among Slovenian children.

title: SUPPRESSION ACTIVITY OF T‐REGULATORY CELLS IN COELIAC DISEASE
abstract: Autoimmunity is prevented by central and peripheral mechanisms of tolerance, one of them is mediated by suppression activity of lymphocytes, named CD4+CD25+T regulatory cells (Treg). This study analized the function of Treg cells in coeliacs. CD4+T cells were isolated from peripheral-blood monocites cells (PBMC) of 6 untreated patients and 5 healthy controls.CD4+CD25-effector cells and Treg cells were separated from CD4+T cells by using CD25 microbeads. To evaluate suppressor activity, effector cells and Treg were co-cultured and stimulated by soluble anti CD3 and anti CD28. Effector cells were prestained with CFSE dye in order to quantify cellular proliferation. After four days of culture, cells were incubated with anti-CD4 and anti-CD25 and analysed by flow cytometry. Our preliminary data shown no difference of immunophenotype and rappresentativness of Treg cells between CD patients and controls. A down regulation activity of patients' Tregs in suppressing T-cell proliferation (−24,3%) versus controls (21,4%) was observed (Fig. 1). Our T regulatory cells studies demonstrated that Tregs cells from celiac patients are deficient in their suppressor activity and also support an overproliferation of T effector cells. About coeliac disease we known genetic predisposition (HLA), exogenous antigen trigger (gluten) and the autoantigen (tTG) but a lot of features are still now unknown. The incorrect activity of Treg population may play a key role in the pathogenesis of CD.

title: HOST IL8 RESPONSE TO PATHOGENIC AND NON‐PATHOGENIC BACTERIA IN VITROPLEMENTARY FOOD WITH BIOACTIVE MILK FAT GLOBULE MEMBRANE PROTEINS
abstract: The acute inflammatory response to bacterial infection is an important part of host defences. This is mediated by NFkB activation inducing an IL-8 response that stimulates neutrophil infliltration. This pathway is also implicated in inflammatory bowel disease and may represent an inappropriate reaction to the normal flora. We aimed to set up an in vitro model of bacterial stimulation of IL-8 production, to compare bacterial species, and to determine virulence factors that influence the host IL-8 response. HEp-2 cells and non-polarised (NPCC) and polarised (PCC) Caco-2 cell lines were exposed to IL-1beta and a prototypic enteropathogenic E coli strain E2348/69 (E69) over a 6 hour period. Cell IL-8 transcriptional activity was measured by RT-PCR; ELISA was used to measure IL-8 protein in culture supernatants. HEp-2 cells were then exposed to a range of bacteria (K12 E coli, B thetaiotamicron, Lactobacilli, and mutant strains of E69 [signalling negative, non-motile, non-adherent]). Il-1 beta produced increased IL-8 mRNA and IL-8 protein in all cell lines. Levels decreased from HEp-2 to NPCC to PCC. E69 induced a rise in IL-8 RNA and protein by 4-6 hours in HEp-2 and NPCC but not in PCC. There was a variable IL-8 response to non-pathogenic bacteria. Deletions in E69 of flagella, bundle forming pili, and type three secretion system structural genes reduced the HEp-2 cell IL-8 response. In comparison lifA and espF deletions enhanced IL-8 levels. A model of IL-8 response to bacterial exposure has been established. Non-pathogenic bacteria can invoke an IL-8 response. EPEC flagella and adhesins induce IL-8, but EPEC appear to have the ability to reduce the IL-8 response. Bacteria cannot be simply divided into “good” and “bad” strains. EPEC possess factors that both upregulate and down regulate the host IL-8 response. The regulated expression of such factors will modulate the host IL-8 response.

title: EPIGENETIC ALTERATIONS IN RESPONSE TO MULTI-WALLED CARBON NANOTUBES AND DHA DIET MODIFICATION
abstract: Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are a class of engineered nanomaterials that pose airborne exposure risks to human health. Immense variations in physical properties such as size and shape complicate understanding the underlying mechanisms and consequences of MWCNT exposures. There are concerns that exposures can lead to chronic pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis diseases, as is the case with other more known ultra-fine respirable materials with similar physical properties, such as crystalline silica and asbestos. Pro-inflammatory diseases can be regulated by epigenetic changes, which can be influenced by environment, including diet. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is an omega-3 fatty acid that may promote resolution of MWCNT- induced inflammation though epigenetic changes, although studies are limited in understanding this process. In Aim 1 of this project, epigenetic changes in lungs were compared in response to varied MWCNT exposures from a single oropharyngeal dose in adult C57Bl/6 mice to "Narrow Short" (NS), "Wide Short" (WS), or "Narrow Long" (NL). MWCNTs were hypothesized to induce differences in epigenetic changes corresponding to severity in physiological and immunological alterations: DM (Dispersion Media/Control) Changes in gene-specific methylation corresponded to acute inflammatory responses preceding excessive collagen growth, influenced by MWCNT size/shape properties. Methylation patterns were observed in conjunction with dysregulated miRNA expression which could help position the immune response to variably downregulate inflammation and upregulate tissue remodeling within the acute to sub-chronic interval. After 56d, no differences in airway thickening were observed, which corresponded to the absence of significant differences in gene-specific methylation among MWCNT groups. Collectively, these findings indicate that MWCNT size/shape can influence acute and sub-chronic post-exposure epigenetic alterations corresponding to progression of acute inflammation in lungs. In Aim 2, to identify potential epigenetic biomarkers of DHA diet modification in response to MWCNT exposure, epigenetic changes were measured using the same methylation and miRNA experimental approaches as in Aim 1. Adult Balb/c mice were fed either a control diet or a 1% DHA-enriched diet before delivery of FA21 (a pro-inflammatory MWCNT) or crystalline silica to determine dysregulated methylation patterns in lungs at 24h (4 weeks of continuous diet) and at 7d post-exposure (5 weeks of continuous diet). miRNA profiling and target predictions were conducted to assess 24h FA21 responses after DHA diet. DHA appeared to offset particle-induced hypomethylation and influenced particle-induced promoter methylation changes 24h and 7d to variable extents. Dysregulated miRNA expression patterns were observed in FA21 exposures and in response to DHA diet. These findings could be beneficial in identifying potential DHA and particle exposure epigenetic biomarkers and could have mechanistic importance in respiratory disease.

title: Integrative strategies and future perspectives to mitigate chemical toxicity in human and aquatic systems
abstract: Human exposure to hazardous chemicals occurs through multiple pathways, including inhalation, ingestion, dermal contact, and consumption of contaminated water, leading to adverse outcomes such as systemic toxicity, and chronic diseases. The release of these contaminants into aquatic ecosystems primarily from industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, and urban effluents has significant ecological ramifications. This review aims to synthesize recent findings on the sources, pathways, toxicological impacts, and mitigation strategies related to chemical pollutants in aquatic environments and human health. A structured literature review was conducted using databases including Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and ResearchGate, with search terms such as “chemical toxicity,” “heavy metal contamination,” “microplastic bioaccumulation,” “aquatic toxicity and health,” “bioremediation of pollutants,” and “green chemistry.” Findings reveal that prolonged exposure to toxic substances is linked to tumors, immune suppression, reproductive dysfunction, developmental delays, and congenital anomalies in humans. Aquatic organisms are similarly impacted by pollutants from pharmaceuticals, pesticides, oil derivatives, and antifouling agents, with documented cases of endocrine disruption and teratogenic effects. Environmental chemical toxicity management still faces major obstacles despite advancements in risk assessment, chemical monitoring, and mitigation techniques. Analytical limitations continue to limit the detection of new pollutants at trace levels, and complicated exposure pathways and mixing effects make estimates of ecological and human risk more difficult. Advanced cleanup methods may be expensive or challenging to apply at scale, and regulatory regimes are sometimes varied across areas. Furthermore, less is known about the long-term, chronic, and synergistic consequences of low-dose exposures, underscoring the necessity of integrated, interdisciplinary methods. This study notably tackles the research gap by integrating human health outcomes with aquatic toxicological information and emphasizing new sustainable mitigation solutions from a unified chemical management viewpoint.
